facts.statehood_note: One of the original 13; New York ratified the U.S. Constitution on July 26, 1788, becoming the 11th state.
facts.name_origin: Named for the Duke of York (later King James II of England), whose forces took the Dutch town of New Amsterdam in 1664.

government.chambers: New York State Senate (currently 63 members) and New York State Assembly (150 members); members of both are elected for two-year terms.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term). The governor is the chief executive and commander-in-chief of the state's military forces, sends the Legislature a yearly budget, signs or vetoes bills, and can grant pardons. The lieutenant governor is elected for the same term and serves as President of the State Senate.
government.courts: Court of Appeals, the highest court (a chief judge and six associate judges, seven in all), appointed by the governor from a nominating commission's list with the Senate's consent, for 14-year terms. In New York, the 'Supreme Court' is a trial court, not the top court.
government.local: 62 counties, plus city, town, and village governments.
government.constitution: New York has had five constitutions: 1777 (adopted April 20, during the Revolution), 1821, 1846, 1894, and 1938. The current constitution is the 1938 one, amended many times since; in 2021 voters added a right to clean air and water, and in 2024 voters expanded the equal protection section (in effect January 1, 2025).
government.kid_line: "No person shall be denied the equal protection of the laws of this state or any subdivision thereof." (New York Constitution, Article I, Section 11(a), as amended by voters in 2024)

long_ago.about: Ganondagan, in today's Victor, was one of the four main Seneca towns in 1687, with bark longhouses for families and a large hilltop granary called Fort Hill.
With the Seneca, these nations formed the League of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois Confederacy), the Five Nations. The Tuscarora later joined, making it the Six Nations.
An Algonquian people who lived in what is now New York when Europeans arrived. Today the Delaware Nation and the Delaware Tribe of Indians are in Oklahoma.
The Mohican lived in what is now New York when Europeans arrived. Many Mohican descendants are part of the Stockbridge-Munsee Community in Wisconsin today.

long_ago.nation: Shinnecock, Montauk, Unkechaug, and other Long Island nations
long_ago.about: Algonquian peoples, including the Shinnecock, Montauk, Unkechaug, Setauket, and Matinecock, lived across Long Island.

today.about: A federally recognized Seneca nation of the Haudenosaunee.
A federally recognized Seneca nation; in the 1800s its people won court cases that helped them buy back more than 7,000 acres of homeland.
A federally recognized Haudenosaunee nation with its own territory in New York.
A federally recognized nation, the sixth nation to join the Haudenosaunee.
A federally recognized Mohawk nation with its own territory in New York.
A federally recognized nation on Long Island.

first_peoples.today_note: New York has eight federally recognized nations: the Cayuga Nation, Oneida Indian Nation, Onondaga Nation, Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe, Seneca Nation of Indians, Shinnecock Indian Nation, Tonawanda Band of Seneca, and Tuscarora Nation. The state also recognizes the Unkechaug Indian Nation on Long Island. Other nations who lost their New York homelands now live elsewhere, such as the Seneca-Cayuga Nation and the Delaware (Lenape) in Oklahoma and the Stockbridge-Munsee (Mohican) and Brothertown (Montauk) in Wisconsin.
sites: Ganondagan State Historic Site in Victor, the original site of a 1600s Seneca town, with a full-size Seneca Bark Longhouse and the Seneca Art and Culture Center

history.event: Indigenous peoples are living in the land now called New York, with early settlement around Lake Champlain, the Hudson River Valley, and Oneida Lake.
Deganawidah, the Onondaga leader Hiawatha, and Jikonsaseh, the 'Mother of Nations,' found the League of the Haudenosaunee, uniting the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca.
Henry Hudson, sailing for the Dutch, explores far up the Hudson River in 1609. The Dutch colony of New Netherland is set up in 1624.
Traders bring the first enslaved Africans to the Dutch town of New Amsterdam.
Eleven enslaved African men petition the Dutch and win partial freedom and more than 100 acres of land, known as 'the Land of the Blacks.'
English forces take New Amsterdam without a fight and rename it New York. Slave laws grow harsher under English rule.
French soldiers burn the Seneca town of Ganondagan, and many Seneca then ally with the British.

Africans are banned from the city's public cemetery, so about 15,000 Africans and people of African descent are buried in the African Burial Ground in Manhattan. Before the Revolution, New York City holds more enslaved Africans than any city except Charleston, South Carolina.
New York adopts its first constitution in April, and in October the Patriots win the Battle of Saratoga, a turning point of the American Revolution.
New York ratifies the U.S. Constitution and becomes the 11th state.
A 1799 law frees children born to enslaved mothers only when they reach age 25 or 28. A later law finally ends slavery in New York on July 4, 1827. Sojourner Truth walks to freedom in 1826.
Women's rights activists hold a convention at Seneca Falls.
New York sends many soldiers and supplies to the Union army. At Appomattox on April 9, 1865, Seneca officer Ely S. Parker writes out the official surrender terms.

trailblazers.name: Jikonsaseh
trailblazers.text: Jikonsaseh is honored as the 'Peace Mother' and the Haudenosaunee 'Mother of Nations.' She helped Hiawatha and Deganawidah create the League of the Haudenosaunee, and Seneca traditionalists connect the name of Ganondagan, 'Town of Peace,' to her.

trailblazers.name: Hiawatha
trailblazers.text: Hiawatha, an Onondaga chief, worked with Deganawidah to unite the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca into the League of the Haudenosaunee, also called the Iroquois Confederacy.

trailblazers.name: Sojourner Truth
trailblazers.text: Sojourner Truth was born enslaved in 1797 in the Town of Esopus in Ulster County, and her first language was Dutch. In 1826 she walked to freedom with her baby daughter Sophie, and in 1828 she sued and won back her young son Peter, who had been illegally sold to an Alabama enslaver, one of the first times a Black woman won such a case against a white man in a U.S. court. She became a leader for abolition and women's rights.

trailblazers.name: Ely S. Parker
trailblazers.text: Born on the Tonawanda Seneca Reservation, Ely S. Parker was refused a law license because Native people were not counted as citizens, so he became an engineer on the Erie Canal. He helped the Tonawanda Seneca fight in court for their homeland, wrote out the surrender terms at Appomattox in 1865 as an aide to General Grant, and became the first Native American Commissioner of Indian Affairs.

trailblazers.name: Harriet Tubman
trailblazers.text: After escaping slavery in Maryland and guiding more than 70 people to freedom, Harriet Tubman made her home with her extended family in Auburn, New York. There she worked for women's right to vote and founded a home for elderly and poor people.

landforms: Catskill Mountains (part of the Appalachian range)
Mount Marcy (5,344 feet) in Essex County, the highest point
Niagara Falls on the border with Ontario
waters: The eleven Finger Lakes, including Seneca and Cayuga Lakes
geography.regions: New York has mountains in the north and west (the Adirondacks and Catskills), the Hudson River Valley in the east, the Finger Lakes in the west, a plain along Lake Erie, and Long Island and the Atlantic coast in the southeast.

ecosystems.name: Forests and mountains
ecosystems.about: Nearly two-thirds of New York is still wooded. Wildlife includes black bears, deer, red foxes, river otters, the beaver (the state animal), and over 470 kinds of birds, including the bald eagle.

ecosystems.name: Lakes and streams
ecosystems.about: New York has eleven Finger Lakes plus Lake Champlain, Lake George, and two Great Lakes. Brook trout, the state freshwater fish, live in its waters, and trout farming is an important business.

ecosystems.name: Atlantic Ocean and Long Island coast
ecosystems.about: Right, finback, and humpback whales swim off New York's Atlantic coast, and Fire Island National Seashore on Long Island is protected by the National Park Service.

science.weather: New York has four seasons. Lake-effect snow buries northern and western areas (Syracuse averages over 120 inches a year), nor'easters bring heavy snow to New York City, and hurricanes can strike the coast, as Hurricane Sandy did in 2012. Sea level along the coast rose about 13 inches from the late 1800s to the 2010s.
science.resources: New York's economy includes finance, publishing, the arts, tourism, and manufacturing, plus farms producing dairy, apples, and wine. Natural resources include clay, salt, and crushed stone, and hydropower is a major energy source.
science.highlight: Lake-effect snow: snow linked to the Great Lakes falls hardest on northern and western New York, and Syracuse averages more than 120 inches of snow a year.

g3_ss.title: New York's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Albany, New York City, and the 62 counties on a map, learn the motto Excelsior (Ever Upward), and meet the Senate and the 150-member Assembly.

g3_ss.title: The Haudenosaunee and Other First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Explore a Seneca bark longhouse at Ganondagan, learn the Five Nations of the Haudenosaunee, and meet the Lenape, Mohican, and Shinnecock.

g3_ss.title: New York Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Make storyboards about Jikonsaseh, Sojourner Truth, Ely S. Parker, and Harriet Tubman.

g45_ss.title: New York's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Study the founding of the League of the Haudenosaunee, life in Seneca towns like Ganondagan, and the eight federally recognized nations in New York today.

g45_ss.title: New Netherland to New York
g45_ss.plan: Compare Dutch and English rule, the 1644 'Land of the Blacks,' slavery and the African Burial Ground, and the 1687 attack on Ganondagan.

g45_ss.title: New York 1777–1877
g45_ss.plan: Trace the 1777 constitution, Saratoga, statehood, the slow end of slavery by 1827, Sojourner Truth's court case, the Erie Canal, Seneca Falls, and Ely S. Parker at Appomattox.

g3_sci.title: Busy Beavers
g3_sci.plan: Learn how the state animal builds dams and lodges and changes streams for other living things.

g3_sci.title: Snow Days
g3_sci.plan: Use a simple model to show how lake-effect snow forms, then compare snowfall in Syracuse with your town.

g3_sci.title: Bluebirds and Sugar Maples
g3_sci.plan: Observe the state bird and state tree and track how a sugar maple changes through the four seasons.

g45_sci.title: The Great Lakes and Lake-Effect Snow
g45_sci.plan: Investigate how water temperature and wind direction create lake-effect snow and map which regions get the most.

g45_sci.title: Mountains, Lakes, and Falls
g45_sci.plan: Map the Adirondacks, Catskills, Finger Lakes, and Niagara Falls, and research how water and ice shaped them.

g45_sci.title: Coasts and Rising Seas
g45_sci.plan: Graph the roughly 13-inch rise in New York's sea level and study how storms like Hurricane Sandy affected Long Island.
